Mindat Formula Note: The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

Mindat Formula Note: The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

Mindat Formula Note:
The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

As it is not explicit if all "O11" sites can be occupied by F in the ideal end-member, the use of (F,OH) is retained here.

Mindat Formula Note:
The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

Note that because the Y3 site occupancy of "end-member" hongheite has not been explicitly defined, and that based on other vesuvianite-group minerals it could be likely considered as either (Fe<sup>3+</sup><sub>4</sub>Mg<sub>4</sub>) or (Fe<sup>3+</sup><sub>6</sub>Mg<sub>2</sub>) (with charge-balancing concomitant occupancy of the "O11" position as [OH]<sub>9</sub> or [(OH)<sub>7</sub>O<sub>2</sub>], respectively), the more generic occupancies denoted by (Fe<sup>3+</sup>,Mg)<sub>8</sub> and (OH,O)<sub>9</sub> have been maintained here, pending further data.

Previously, the mineral "hibschite" (no longer an IMA-approved species) was considered an intermediate member of the grossular-katoite series, and was defined as Ca<sub>3</sub>Al<sub>2</sub>(SiO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3-x</sub>(OH)<sub>4x</sub>, where x = 0.2-1.5; compositions where x < 0.2 were still considered grossular, whereas compositions where x > 1.5 were considered katoite. Now, based on the modern "50% rule", what was previously called "hibschite" would now be considered grossular (or perhaps more descriptively as "OH-bearing grossular"), although "hibschite", "hydrogrossular" and "hydrogarnet" are still all informally in common use.

Mindat IMA History:
Based on [[1| Brögger, W.C., Bäckström, H., 1891]] the name lazurite was grandfathered by the IMA who later gave it Hassan's ideal formula, Na<sub>3</sub>Ca(Si<sub>3</sub>Al<sub>3</sub>)O<sub>12</sub>S [[2|Hassan et al., 1985]]. The data used by Hassan all came from <m>haüyne</m>s with approximately Na<sub>6</sub>Ca<sub>2</sub>(Al<sub>6</sub>Si<sub>6</sub>O<sub>24</sub>)(SO<sub>4</sub>,S,Cl,OH)<sub>2</sub> as no sulfide-dominant mineral required by Hassan's formula had been observed. 

The situation was similar to <m>sodalite</m> and <m>hackmanite</m> defined as a sulfur dominant <m>sodalite</m> which was never found. In <m>sodalite</m>, Cl is the dominant cage filler and such an ideal <m>hackmanite</m> would have S as the cage filler. Though S readily substitutes for Cl in <m>sodalite</m>, no sulfide-dominant species was ever observed. On that basis, <m>hackmanite</m> was never approved, avoiding the approval of a hypothetical mineral. Before the 2021 redefinition, the situation was reversed with lazurite and <m>haüyne</m>. What was commonly called lazurite, all had dominant SO<sub>4</sub> and were sulfide-rich <m>haüyne</m>s, just as all <m>hackmanite</m>s were sulfide-rich <m>sodalite</m>s. Now <m>hackmanite</m> is defined as a reversible photochromic variety of <m>sodalite</m>.

The redefinition of lazurite as <m>haüyne</m> with just more than a quarter of its cages containing sulfide is due to acceptance of the proposal 20-H (Newsletter #60). The neotype specimen originates from the Malo-Bystrinskoe <m>lazurite</m> deposit, Baikal Lake area, eastern Siberia, Russia, and was published by Sapozhnikov et al. (2021).

Mindat Formula Note: The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

Mindat Formula Note:
The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

Note that in lieu of published structural data, the Y2 and Y3 site occupancies denoted here are distributed as per other members of the other vesuvianite group minerals (i.e. Y2 = Al-dominant; Ti & Fe<sup>3+</sup> assigned to Y3). These occupancies may be re-assigned with updated data.  Justification for the -(REE) suffix is that REE (in this case predominately Ce) is the dominant cation in the X3 site.

Mindat Formula Note: The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)2(X3)8(X2)8(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca19) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M2+ and M3+ ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO4) may be replaced by (H4O4), akin to the Si4+ ↔︎ 4H+ hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M2+ cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied. Note that although the IMA formula denotes the end-member Y3 site filling as (Al6Mg2), the composition of the most Mn-rich sample reported in Armbruster et al., 2002 (sample NC-14-38) more closely conforms to a Y3 site filling of (Mn3+4Al2Mn2+2).

Mindat Formula Note: According to Mössbauer data, all iron in the mineral is trivalent. The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)2(X3)8(X2)8(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca19) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M2+ and M3+ ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO4) may be replaced by (H4O4), akin to the Si4+ ↔︎ 4H+ hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M2+ cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied. Note: The published formula by Chukanov et al. (2019) includes ∑(REE+Y) = 1.97 apfu (primarily in the X3 site), although this amount does not dominate the site and so might be disregarded when considering the end-member formula. However, the extra charge afforded by this REE inclusion appears necessary to provide charge balance for defining M2+>M3+ in the Y3 site, as full hydrogenation of the "O10" and "O11" positions would be otherwise insufficient. To address this inconsistency and to closer approximate the published analysis, one apfu of REE is included in the presented formula to maintain charge balance (although other charge-balancing mechanisms, such as the addition of B into the normally vacant T1 and/or T2 sites, may also be possible).

Mindat IMA History:
IMA No. 2017-086
Named changed in 2024 (IMA Newsletter 77):
"It was agreed to modify the name straßmannite to strassmannite, with “double s” instead of ß – the so-called “Eszett” which is peculiar of the German alphabet. This is in keeping with a recent CNMNC resolution [Mineralogical Magazine, 87, 225-232 (2023)] which aims at rationalising the mineralogical nomenclature by abolishing Greek letters as well as Arabic and Roman numerals from mineral names. Straßmannite represented the unique case among mineral names in which the Eszett was employed instead of double s. Therefore, for the sake of analogy with fleisstalite, giessenite, günterblassite, mössbauerite, phosphorrösslerite and rösslerite, the mineral straßmannite – which was approved only six years ago – is now renamed strassmannite. This is an executive decision taken by the CNMNC officers."

Mindat Formula Note: The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen atoms that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

Mindat Formula Note:
The formula is a partial simplification of the full structural formula. The large (VII-IX)-coordinated (X4)<sub>2</sub>(X3)<sub>8</sub>(X2)<sub>8</sub>(X1) sites are here combined (e.g. Ca<sub>19</sub>) and are typically filled with Ca, although other large cations such as the REE may be present. The square-pyramidal Y1 site can host a variety of M<sup>2+</sup> and M<sup>3+</sup> ions and is the basis for the distinction of several species. The VI-coordinated Y2 site typically is filled with Al, whereas the also VI-coordinated Y3 site may contain Al, Mg, and other cations of similar charge and size. The tetrahedral T1 site is typically vacant but may contain B (less commonly Al); the trigonal T2 site is also typically vacant but may also contain B. Some of the (SiO<sub>4</sub>) may be replaced by (H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), akin to the Si<sup>4+</sup> ↔︎ 4H<sup>+</sup> hydrogarnet substitution. Among the oxygen that are not part of the silica tetrahedra, there are eight "O11" that typically occur as OH, two "O10" that are typically O & OH or OH & OH (the latter arrangement notably when Y1 is an M<sup>2+</sup> cation). There may also be up to three "O12" that in most vesuvianite-group minerals are absent (and are not included here), but may be present particularly when T1 is occupied.

With increased filling of the T2 site by B, various charge balance mechanisms involving either increased O for OH in the "O11" position and/or increased M<sup>2+</sup> for M<sup>3+</sup> substitution in the Y3 site are necessary (see idealized formula for full T2 occupancy by B). In lieu of an explicitly defined "end-member" wiluite, more generic representations of site fillings are retained here, pending newer data.
